nameStory: The name 'fleabane' comes from the old belief that these plants could repel fleas when burned or scattered around homes. 'Daisy fleabane' refers to its small daisy-like flowers, though it's much tinier than the classic white daisies we know. Whether it actually worked against fleas is questionable, but the name stuck through centuries of folk use.
description: Daisy fleabane is a scrappy annual wildflower that looks like someone scattered hundreds of tiny white daisies across a branching plant. Each flower head is smaller than your pinky nail, with thread-thin white petals (sometimes tinged pink or blue) surrounding a yellow center. The plant can grow up to 32 inches tall, with most of its oval leaves clustered near the bottom and an intricate network of thin stems branching out above.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dozens to hundreds of tiny flower heads, each less than half an inch wide, with 50-100 extremely narrow white, pink, or blue ray petals surrounding yellow centers - they feel delicate and papery to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Spindly, much-branched stems create an airy, open appearance in the upper portion, like a botanical chandelier spreading outward

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Hairy, oval-shaped leaves concentrated mostly on the lower half of the plant, feeling slightly rough and fuzzy when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, wiry stems covered in short, stiff hairs that give them a slightly rough texture - the branching becomes increasingly intricate toward the top

habitat: Daisy fleabane thrives in disturbed soils and open areas throughout New England, from roadsides and old fields to gardens and vacant lots. You'll often find it in poor, dry soils where other plants struggle, making it a common sight along trails, in meadows, and at forest edges. It's particularly fond of sunny spots with well-drained soil.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of hairy, oval leaves close to the ground. The distinctive branching flower stems haven't yet developed.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season when the characteristic cloud of tiny white daisy-like flowers appears. The intricate branching structure becomes most obvious now.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue into early fall, eventually producing small seeds with white bristles that blow away in the wind. Plants begin to brown and dry out.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only dried brown stems that may persist. Seeds lie dormant in the soil until spring.

funFact: A single daisy fleabane plant can produce up to 200 flower heads, and each tiny flower head contains as many as 100 individual ray petals - meaning one small plant might display 20,000 petals at once, making it one of the most petal-dense wildflowers in New England!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with annual fleabane, which has wider flower heads and broader petals. Remember: daisy fleabane has thread-thin petals that look almost grass-like, while annual fleabane has more substantial, daisy-like petals. Think 'thin as thread' for daisy fleabane.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, fleabane belongs to the same family as sunflowers and true daisies, but it's not closely related to either. The 'fleabane' name is shared by several different plants that were all thought to repel insects, creating some confusion among common names.
compareHints: Daisy fleabane differs from its fleabane cousins by having the narrowest ray petals - they're almost thread-like compared to the broader petals of annual fleabane or Philadelphia fleabane. Horseweed has even tinier, less noticeable petals and a more column-like growth habit. Robin's plantain blooms much earlier in spring with fewer, larger flower heads.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its showier cousins like daisy fleabane and annual fleabane, horseweed has extremely small, inconspicuous flowers that barely look like typical daisy-family blooms.
Among its fleabane relatives, robin's plantain stands out as the earliest bloomer with the most robust appearance and widest petals.
Among New England fleabanes, annual fleabane is distinguished by its relatively wide, obvious white petals and robust growth habit.
Among New England's fleabanes, Philadelphia fleabane stands out with its extremely numerous thread-like petals (50-150) compared to daisy fleabane's fewer, broader petals (typically under 50).
Unlike the much more common daisy fleabane and annual fleabane which form branching clusters of many small flowers, hyssop-leaved fleabane usually produces just one flower head per stem.
Coulter's fleabane differs from common New England fleabanes by having fewer but larger flower heads and more robust growth.
